e-11151.knowledge_point: Mapping an Area to a Rectangular Region: Transformations Given
e-11151.problem:
Using the change of variables

$$
u = \dfrac{y^2}{x}, \qquad v= xy,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the curves

$$
x = {y^2}, \qquad x=\dfrac{y^2}3, \qquad y=\dfrac2x, \qquad y=\dfrac4x.
$$
e-11151.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y.
$$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as follows: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/e4acf61532998ca5b0768b7edde16be779298c1be15ef11b14472678ba43043a.png)

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u = \dfrac{y^2}{x}, \qquad v= xy
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/3706f0373bb39ebd41d78dd453896548ec03638a656e1fe36604f2a43108ba8e.png)

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u= \dfrac{y^2}{x}$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & x={y}^{2} & ⟹\, & \frac{{y}^{2}}{x}=1 & ⟹\, & u=1 \\  & x=\frac{{y}^{2}}{3} & ⟹\, & \frac{{y}^{2}}{x}=3 & ⟹\, & u=3\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v = xy$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{2}{x} & ⟹\, & xy=2 & ⟹\, & v=2 \\  & y=\frac{4}{x} & ⟹\, & xy=4 & ⟹\, & v=4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 1 \leq u \leq 3, \quad 2 \leq v \leq 4\big\}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/1207d8cdb8afd7c55d712caca043edfe9f0d0395343a6cbd329cf5861ec3bce7.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{2y}{x} \\ y & \text{ }\text{ }x\end{aligned}| \\  & =-\frac{3{y}^{2}}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = -\dfrac{x}{3y^2} = -\dfrac{1}{3u}.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$  In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{3u}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\cdot (4-2) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

e-11154.knowledge_point: Mapping an Area to a Rectangular Region: Transformations Not Given
e-11154.problem:
Use a change of variables to calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the following curves.

$$
e^y = \dfrac{5}{e^x}, \qquad e^y=\dfrac{10}{e^x}, \qquad e^x=e^y, \qquad e^x=2e^y
$$
e-11154.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y.
$$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as follows: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/f47c1b7ce7e9073a10c2665821a4fc0d5b38ce6ad6c0f79a75a5b203962112cd.png)

We'll assume this transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v,
$$

  

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

To compute the required area, we proceed in five steps:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

Notice that we can rewrite the equations of our curves as follows:

$$
e^{x+y} = 5, \qquad e^{x+y}=10, \qquad e^{x-y} = 1, \qquad e^{x-y} = 2
$$

This suggests the following change of variables:

$$
u = e^{x+y}, \qquad v = e^{x-y}
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/88c92ebc206481c3ef86661ee413358bb060cb85f642148c609de0bf1a9da2d1.png)

**Step 2**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=e^{x+y}$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {e}^{x+y}=5\,⟹\,u=5 \\  & {e}^{x+y}=10\,⟹\,u=10\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v =e^{x-y}$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {e}^{x-y}=1\,⟹\,v=1 \\  & {e}^{x-y}=2\,⟹\,v=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 5 \leq u \leq 10, \quad 1 \leq v \leq 2\big\}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/105745a82e8f67b086f526b0166e3b442d3eaf02e4df69314ed9d3ffd5fca071.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+y} & {e}^{x+y} \\ {e}^{x-y} & -{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =-{e}^{2x}-{e}^{2x} \\  & =-2{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} =  -\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-2x}=-\dfrac{1}{2uv}.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)}\neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$  In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 5**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{2uv}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{uv}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{5}^{10}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡10-\operatorname{ln}⁡5)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

e-7283.knowledge_point: Finding an Area by Transforming to a Type I Region
e-7283.problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u =3x-2y, \quad v=x+y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(3x-2y)^2 - y - x = 0$ and the line $x+y=4.$
e-7283.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y.
$$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as follows: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/87b44aa661a51ee39011c33c2eb000edcebb127508d45d5819339cf532258f3e.png)

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u = 3x-2y, \qquad v=x+y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/88c92ebc206481c3ef86661ee413358bb060cb85f642148c609de0bf1a9da2d1.png)

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $3x-2y = u$ and $x+y = v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x-2y)^{2}-y-x=0\,⟹\,{u}^{2}-v=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $x + y = v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y+x=4\,⟹\,v=4.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v={u}^{2} \\ v=4\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=\pm 2 \\ v=4.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 2, 4).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: -2 \leq u \leq 2, \, u^2 \leq v \leq 4\big\},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/0a3d0211dfbe18e5737b62e8b61cf9308af2735ef827d14bae7b5dbfffaa4faa.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = (5)^{-1} = \dfrac 15.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$  In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}[{\int }_{{u}^{2}}^{4}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}[v]_{{u}^{2}}^{4}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}(4-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot 2{\int }_{0}^{2}(4-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{[4u-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(8-\frac{8}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(\frac{16}{3}) \\  & =\frac{32}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The boundaries become 2 ≤ u ≤ 3 and 1 ≤ v ≤ 3. From x=uv and y=1/(u²v), the absolute Jacobian is 1/(u²v). Thus the area is ∫₂³ u⁻² du · ∫₁³ v⁻¹ dv = (1/2−1/3)ln(3) = ln(3)/6.

after.problem:
Using the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{1}{xy},\,v={x}^{2}y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the curves

$$
y=\frac{1}{2x},\,y=\frac{1}{3x},\,y=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\,y=\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}.
$$
after.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=\frac{1}{xy},\,v={x}^{2}y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=\frac{1}{xy}$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{2x} & ⟹\, & \frac{1}{xy}=2 & ⟹\, & u=2 \\  & y=\frac{1}{3x} & ⟹\, & \frac{1}{xy}=3 & ⟹\, & u=3\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v={x}^{2}y$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & ⟹\, & {x}^{2}y=1 & ⟹\, & v=1 \\  & y=\frac{3}{{x}^{2}} & ⟹\, & {x}^{2}y=3 & ⟹\, & v=3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 3,\,1\le v\le 3}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/05d2ca47db245b147cb52f95a474a60ece144931c8b6e1e40c6628a99b53d690.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y} & -\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}} \\ 2xy & \text{ }\text{ }{x}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=y=\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}y}=\frac{1}{{u}^{2}v}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$

$$

content.problem:
Using the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{1}{xy},\,v={x}^{2}y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the curves

$$
y=\frac{1}{2x},\,y=\frac{1}{3x},\,y=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\,y=\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}.
$$
content.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=\frac{1}{xy},\,v={x}^{2}y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=\frac{1}{xy}$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{2x} & ⟹\, & \frac{1}{xy}=2 & ⟹\, & u=2 \\  & y=\frac{1}{3x} & ⟹\, & \frac{1}{xy}=3 & ⟹\, & u=3\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v={x}^{2}y$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & ⟹\, & {x}^{2}y=1 & ⟹\, & v=1 \\  & y=\frac{3}{{x}^{2}} & ⟹\, & {x}^{2}y=3 & ⟹\, & v=3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 3,\,1\le v\le 3}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/05d2ca47db245b147cb52f95a474a60ece144931c8b6e1e40c6628a99b53d690.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y} & -\frac{1}{x{y}^{2}} \\ 2xy & \text{ }\text{ }{x}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=y=\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}y}=\frac{1}{{u}^{2}v}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{{u}^{2}v}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}v}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =(-\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{2})\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=y-3x,\,v=y+2x,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the lines

$$
y=3x-2,\,y=3x+2,\,y=1-2x,\,y=3-2x.
$$
after.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=y-3x,\,v=y+2x
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=y-3x$ into the equations of the first and second lines:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=3x-2 & ⟹\, & y-3x=-2 & ⟹\, & u=-2 \\  & y=3x+2 & ⟹\, & y-3x=2 & ⟹\, & u=2\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=y+2x$ into the equations of the third and fourth lines:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=1-2x & ⟹\, & y+2x=1 & ⟹\, & v=1 \\  & y=3-2x & ⟹\, & y+2x=3 & ⟹\, & v=3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,-2\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le 3}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/9c17c81b4abc0d4ebd1eadfe951b0eb0c2674d9eb07b785e7fd972fd00e513ae.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 2 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{5}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{5}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{∬}_{Δ}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot \text{Area}(Δ) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot 4\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{8}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=y-3x$ into the equations of the first and second lines:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=3x-2 & ⟹\, & y-3x=-2 & ⟹\, & u=-2 \\  & y=3x+2 & ⟹\, & y-3x=2 & ⟹\, & u=2\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=y+2x$ into the equations of the third and fourth lines:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=1-2x & ⟹\, & y+2x=1 & ⟹\, & v=1 \\  & y=3-2x & ⟹\, & y+2x=3 & ⟹\, & v=3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,-2\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le 3}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/9c17c81b4abc0d4ebd1eadfe951b0eb0c2674d9eb07b785e7fd972fd00e513ae.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 2 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{5}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{5}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{∬}_{Δ}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot \text{Area}(Δ) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot 4\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{8}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Use a change of variables to calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the following curves and lines.

$$
y=\frac{1}{x},\,y=\frac{4}{x},\,x={y}^{2},\,x=3{y}^{2}
$$
after.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

We'll assume this transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv,
$$

  

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required area, we proceed in five steps:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

Notice that we can rewrite the equations of our curves as follows:

$$
xy=1,\,xy=4,\,\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}=1,\,\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}=3
$$

This suggests the following change of variables:

$$
u=xy,\,v=\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=xy$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & xy=1\,⟹\,u=1 \\  & xy=4\,⟹\,u=4\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{x}{{y}^{2}}=1\,⟹\,v=1 \\  & \frac{x}{{y}^{2}}=3\,⟹\,v=3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 4,\,1\le v\le 3}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/2d98eb2de472226d010fb633478f3662754679c2256e3fd3d06600a6599bc7f5.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}y & x \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}} & -\frac{2x}{{y}^{3}}\end{aligned}| \\  & =-\frac{2x}{{y}^{2}}-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{3x}{{y}^{2}} \\  & =-3v.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{3v}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{3v}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{v}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{4}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (4-1)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡3\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{8}.

$$

$$
{x}^{2}y=2,\,{x}^{2}y=4,\,xy=1,\,xy=3
$$

This suggests the following change of variables:

$$
u={x}^{2}y,\,v=xy
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u={x}^{2}y$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{2}y=2\,⟹\,u=2 \\  & {x}^{2}y=4\,⟹\,u=4\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=xy$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & xy=1\,⟹\,v=1 \\  & xy=3\,⟹\,v=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 4,\,1\le v\le 3}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/baa8e8ab6cff8edec84d3f0d0950931f247153523e3320abbdf673161afb44ae.png)

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2xy & {x}^{2} \\ y & x\end{aligned}| \\  & =2{x}^{2}y-{x}^{2}y \\  & =u.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{u}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{1}{u}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}v \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\cdot (3-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}

content.knowledge_point: Mapping an Area to a Rectangular Region: Transformations Not Given
content.problem:
Use a change of variables to calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the following curves and lines.

$$
y=\frac{2}{{x}^{2}},\,y=\frac{4}{{x}^{2}},\,y=\frac{1}{x},\,y=\frac{3}{x}
$$
content.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

We'll assume this transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv,
$$

  

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required area, we proceed in five steps:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

Notice that we can rewrite the equations of our curves as follows:

$$
{x}^{2}y=2,\,{x}^{2}y=4,\,xy=1,\,xy=3
$$

This suggests the following change of variables:

$$
u={x}^{2}y,\,v=xy
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u={x}^{2}y$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{2}y=2\,⟹\,u=2 \\  & {x}^{2}y=4\,⟹\,u=4\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=xy$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & xy=1\,⟹\,v=1 \\  & xy=3\,⟹\,v=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 4,\,1\le v\le 3}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/baa8e8ab6cff8edec84d3f0d0950931f247153523e3320abbdf673161afb44ae.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2xy & {x}^{2} \\ y & x\end{aligned}| \\  & =2{x}^{2}y-{x}^{2}y \\  & =u.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{u}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{1}{u}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}v \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\cdot (3-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
Use a change of variables to calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the following lines.

$$
3y=4x+1,\,3y=4x-2,\,3x=2y+1,\,3x=2y+3
$$
content.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

We'll assume this transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv,
$$

  

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required area, we proceed in five steps:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

Notice that we can rewrite the equations of our curves as follows:

$$
4x-3y=-1,\,4x-3y=2,\,3x-2y=1,\,3x-2y=3
$$

This suggests the following change of variables:

$$
u=4x-3y,\,v=3x-2y
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=4x-3y$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 4x-3y=-1\,⟹\,u=-1 \\  & 4x-3y=2\,⟹\,u=2\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=3x-2y$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 3x-2y=1\,⟹\,v=1 \\  & 3x-2y=3\,⟹\,v=3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le 3}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/5dc4be989300dca3e52b7ff1dfb6a21c60409976fe55d42f5ae530f033725a64.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-8+9 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|1|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}v \\  & =(2-(-1))\cdot (3-1) \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=y+2x,\,v=y-2x
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $y+2x=u$ into the equation of the first line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+2x=1\,⟹\,u=1,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $y-2x=v$ into the equation of the second line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2x=1\,⟹\,v=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $u=y+2x$ and $v=y-2x$ into the equation of curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4{x}^{2}=4\,⟹\,(y+2x)(y-2x)=4,\,⟹\,uv=4.\end{aligned}
$$

The intersection point of the two lines in the $uv$-plane is $(1,1).$

To find the intersection of the curve with the first line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}uv=4 \\ u=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=1 \\ v=4.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the intersections of the curve with the second line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}uv=4 \\ v=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=4 \\ v=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the intersection points are $(1,1),$ $(1,4)$ and $(4,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 4,\,1\le v\le \frac{4}{u}}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/30fff9564451baadff3cae48dbfb91dc08fc8591e596e7cd2f65d8cfc6c9c5a6.png)

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(4)^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Area by Transforming to a Type I Region
content.problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=y+2x,\,v=y-2x,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the lines $y+2x=1,$ $y-2x=1$ and the curve ${y}^{2}-4{x}^{2}=4.$
content.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=y+2x,\,v=y-2x
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $y+2x=u$ into the equation of the first line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+2x=1\,⟹\,u=1,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $y-2x=v$ into the equation of the second line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2x=1\,⟹\,v=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $u=y+2x$ and $v=y-2x$ into the equation of curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4{x}^{2}=4\,⟹\,(y+2x)(y-2x)=4,\,⟹\,uv=4.\end{aligned}
$$

The intersection point of the two lines in the $uv$-plane is $(1,1).$

To find the intersection of the curve with the first line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}uv=4 \\ u=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=1 \\ v=4.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the intersections of the curve with the second line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}uv=4 \\ v=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=4 \\ v=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the intersection points are $(1,1),$ $(1,4)$ and $(4,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 4,\,1\le v\le \frac{4}{u}}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/30fff9564451baadff3cae48dbfb91dc08fc8591e596e7cd2f65d8cfc6c9c5a6.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(4)^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{1}{4}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}[{\int }_{1}^{4/u}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}[v]_{1}^{4/u}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}(\frac{4}{u}-1)du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[4\operatorname{ln}⁡u-u]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(4\operatorname{ln}⁡4-4+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(4\operatorname{ln}⁡4-3) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=x-y,\,v=y+1,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(x-y)^{2}+y=2$ and the line $y=0.$
after.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x-y,\,v=y+1
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x-y=u$ and $y=v+1$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-y)^{2}+y=2\,⟹\,(y+1)=3-(x-y)^{2}\,⟹\,v=3-{u}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

 

while substituting $y=v-1$ into the equation of the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=0\,⟹\,v=1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v=3-{u}^{2} \\ v=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=\pm \sqrt{2} \\ v=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm \sqrt{2},1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,-\sqrt{2}\le u\le \sqrt{2},\,1\le v\le 3-{u}^{2}.}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/9cec7ff29557aa14cd19309e9180482a44091e7ef215205285822674e7bc25b0.png)

 

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}[{\int }_{1}^{3-{u}^{2}}\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}[v]_{1}^{3-{u}^{2}}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}(3-{u}^{2}-1)\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}(2-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & ={[2u-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =(2\sqrt{2}-\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3})-(-2\sqrt{2}+\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}) \\  & =\frac{8\sqrt{2}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

history.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x-y,\,v=y+1
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x-y=u$ and $y=v+1$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-y)^{2}+y=2\,⟹\,(y+1)=3-(x-y)^{2}\,⟹\,v=3-{u}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

 

while substituting $y=v-1$ into the equation of the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=0\,⟹\,v=1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v=3-{u}^{2} \\ v=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=\pm \sqrt{2} \\ v=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm \sqrt{2},1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,-\sqrt{2}\le u\le \sqrt{2},\,1\le v\le 3-{u}^{2}.}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/9cec7ff29557aa14cd19309e9180482a44091e7ef215205285822674e7bc25b0.png)

 

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}[{\int }_{1}^{3-{u}^{2}}\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}[v]_{1}^{3-{u}^{2}}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}(3-{u}^{2}-1)\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}(2-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & ={[2u-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =(2\sqrt{2}-\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3})-(-2\sqrt{2}+\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}) \\  & =\frac{8\sqrt{2}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Now, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}x+y=u \\ x-y=v\end{aligned}\,⟹\,y=\frac{u-v}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this value into the equation of the given line yields:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=0\, & ⟹\,\frac{u-v}{2}=0\,⟹\,v=u\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v={u}^{4} \\ v=u\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{u}^{3}(u-1)=0 \\ v=u.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the intersection points are $(0,0)$ and $(1,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,{u}^{4}\le v\le u}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/1ed905e319e689d3fc7955a30f58e0f3ae2e7a751c27b80201d2b43f58b4206c.png)

$$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(-2)^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{{u}^{4}}^{u}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[v]_{{u}^{4}}^{u}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(u-{u}^{4})du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{u}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{3}{10}) \\  & =\frac{3}{20}\end{aligned}

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Area by Transforming to a Type I Region
content.problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=x+y,\,v=x-y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(x+y)^{4}-x+y=0$ and  the line $y=0.$
content.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x+y,\,v=x-y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x+y=u$ and $x-y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+y)^{4}-x+y=0\,⟹\,(x+y)^{4}-(x-y)=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{4},\end{aligned}
$$

Now, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}x+y=u \\ x-y=v\end{aligned}\,⟹\,y=\frac{u-v}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this value into the equation of the given line yields:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=0\, & ⟹\,\frac{u-v}{2}=0\,⟹\,v=u\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v={u}^{4} \\ v=u\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{u}^{3}(u-1)=0 \\ v=u.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the intersection points are $(0,0)$ and $(1,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,{u}^{4}\le v\le u}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/1ed905e319e689d3fc7955a30f58e0f3ae2e7a751c27b80201d2b43f58b4206c.png)

 

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(-2)^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{{u}^{4}}^{u}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[v]_{{u}^{4}}^{u}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(u-{u}^{4})du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{u}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{3}{10}) \\  & =\frac{3}{20}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The curve becomes v=u²−3 and the line becomes v=1. They intersect at u=±2, enclosing −2≤u≤2 and u²−3≤v≤1. The absolute inverse Jacobian is 1, so the area is ∫₋₂²(4−u²)du=32/3, option a.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Area by Transforming to a Type I Region
content.problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=y+3x,\,v=x,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(y+3x)^{2}-x=3$ and the line $x=1.$
content.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=y+3x,\,v=x
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $y+3x=u$ and $x=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3x)^{2}-x=3\,⟹\,{u}^{2}-v=3\,⟹\,v={u}^{2}-3,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $x=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x=1\,⟹\,v=1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v={u}^{2}-3 \\ v=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=\pm 2 \\ v=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 2,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,-2\le u\le 2,\,{u}^{2}-3\le v\le 1}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/2687f0cc14eb0b476ea5f4ba7272e7f248bb7dcb276a0e2b0c39e551501b011d.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(-1)^{-1}=-1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-1|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}[{\int }_{{u}^{2}-3}^{1}\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}[v]_{{u}^{2}-3}^{1}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}(1-({u}^{2}-3))\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}(4-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & ={[4u-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =16-\frac{16}{3} \\  & =\frac{32}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
u=x-2y,\,v=y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $y-(x-2y)^{2}=2$ and the line $y=3.$
after.worked_solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x-2y,\,v=y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x-2y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(x-2y)^{2}=2\,⟹\,v-{u}^{2}=2\,⟹\,v={u}^{2}+2,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=3\,⟹\,v=3.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}v={u}^{2}+2 \\ v=3\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=\pm 1 \\ v=3.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 1,3).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,{u}^{2}+2\le v\le 3}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095970/assets/ca755cd11609e7c704adb37eb867ff8cc48bc5fc44b29cd777269be5791d9160.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|1|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{{u}^{2}+2}^{3}\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[v]_{{u}^{2}+2}^{3}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(3-({u}^{2}+2))\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(1-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & ={[u-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2-\frac{2}{3} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
